doc.title: Dorothy Donegan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Developing her left hand after Buck and Bubbles
summary: Younger players are learning left hand; Buck and Bubbles told her to play it in the 1930s and it grew stronger than her right.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: You think so? Where do you see that support coming from and how do you see the younger players coming through?
They’re beginning to listen now and they got to learn how to play with the left hand. See, before they didn’t know how to play with the left hand.
Tell me about your left hand, how it developed and how it changed over time.
Well, I was playing in the ‘30’s, so I met Buck and Bubbles. So, they said, “What you gonna do with the left hand?” I said, “I don’t know.” Said, “Did you leave it in the dressing
room? Say, woman, you’ve got to play some left hand.” So I think my left hand got stronger than my right.
